chapter.name: Three Dimensional Geometry
chapter.blurb: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line, including the line through two points, and the vector and Cartesian equations of a line in space. The chapter then finds the angle between two lines with the conditions for perpendicular and parallel lines, and the shortest distance between two skew lines and between two parallel lines.

scope_in.item: State the direction angles and direction cosines l, m, n of a directed line, use l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1, and explain that reversing the direction reverses the signs so an undirected line has two sets of direction cosines; for a line not through the origin use the parallel line through the origin

Define direction ratios as numbers proportional to the direction cosines, know a line has infinitely many proportional sets, and convert direction ratios a, b, c to direction cosines by dividing by +/- sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)
Find direction cosines from given angles with the axes (including the coordinate axes themselves and a line equally inclined to the axes)
Find the direction ratios x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1 and the direction cosines of the line joining two points, dividing by PQ
Show three points are collinear by proportional direction ratios of AB and BC with B common

Write the vector equation r = a + lambda b of a line through a point parallel to a vector, its parametric equations and its Cartesian equation (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c, and convert between the forms
Write the vector equation of the line through two points as r = a + lambda (b - a)
Find the acute angle between two lines from direction ratios, direction cosines, vector equations or Cartesian equations

Use the conditions a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0 for perpendicular lines and a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 for parallel lines, including finding an unknown constant and finding a line perpendicular to two given lines

Describe skew lines (neither parallel nor intersecting, non-coplanar), the angle between skew lines, and the line of shortest distance perpendicular to both; know intersecting lines have shortest distance zero
Find the shortest distance between two skew lines, d = |(b1 x b2) . (a2 - a1)| / |b1 x b2|, from vector or Cartesian equations
Find the distance between two parallel lines, d = |b x (a2 - a1)| / |b|, and recognise when lines are parallel

concepts.name: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line
concepts.description: The direction angles and direction cosines l, m, n of a directed line, the two sets of direction cosines of an undirected line, direction ratios as numbers proportional to the direction cosines, and converting direction ratios to direction cosines.
concepts.idea: A directed line makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the positive x, y and z axes; the cosines of these angles are its direction cosines. Any three numbers proportional to them are direction ratios.
concepts.rule: l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. If a, b, c are direction ratios, then l = a/k, m = b/k, n = c/k with k = sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) or its negative. Reversing the direction reverses all three signs; a line has infinitely many sets of direction ratios.
concepts.example: A line with direction ratios 2, -1, -2 has sqrt(4 + 1 + 4) = 3, so its direction cosines are 2/3, -1/3, -2/3.

questions.a: Let the direction cosines be l, l, l. Then l^2 + l^2 + l^2 = 1, so 3 l^2 = 1 and l = 1/sqrt(3) or -1/sqrt(3). The direction cosines are 1/sqrt(3), 1/sqrt(3), 1/sqrt(3) or -1/sqrt(3), -1/sqrt(3), -1/sqrt(3).
s: Takes l = m = n and uses l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 to get 3 l^2 = 1
Gives the direction cosines as 1/sqrt(3) each (or -1/sqrt(3) each)

questions.q: A line makes an angle of 60 degrees with the x-axis and 45 degrees with the y-axis. Find the possible angles it makes with the z-axis and write the corresponding direction cosines.
questions.a: l = cos 60 = 1/2 and m = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2). From l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1, n^2 = 1 - 1/4 - 1/2 = 1/4, so n = 1/2 or -1/2. The angle with the z-axis is 60 degrees or 120 degrees, and the direction cosines are 1/2, 1/sqrt(2), 1/2 or 1/2, 1/sqrt(2), -1/2.
s: Writes l = 1/2 and m = 1/sqrt(2)
Uses l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 to get n = 1/2 or -1/2
States the angle with the z-axis is 60 or 120 degrees and writes the direction cosines

questions.q: Assertion (A): If a line has direction ratios 3, 4, 12, then 3/13, 4/13, 12/13 is a set of its direction cosines. Reason (R): The direction cosines of a line are obtained by dividing its direction ratios a, b, c by sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2), taken with either sign.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Consider these statements about a line in space. (I) A given line, taken without a chosen direction, has two sets of direction cosines that differ only in sign. (II) A given line has exactly one set of direction ratios. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Can a line make an angle of 45 degrees with each of the three coordinate axes? Analyse using direction cosines, and find the cosine of the angle that a line equally inclined to the three axes actually makes with each axis.
questions.a: If each angle were 45 degrees, then l = m = n = 1/sqrt(2) and l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3/2, which is not 1. So no such line exists. For an equally inclined line, 3 l^2 = 1, so the cosine of the angle with each axis is 1/sqrt(3) (or -1/sqrt(3) for the opposite direction).
s: Finds l = m = n = 1/sqrt(2) and the sum of squares 3/2
Concludes that no such line exists because the sum of squares must be 1
Finds the cosine 1/sqrt(3) (or -1/sqrt(3)) for an equally inclined line

questions.q: A student says: 'A line with direction ratios 1, 2, 2 and a line with direction ratios -2, -4, -4 must point in different directions, because the numbers are different.' Is the student right? Justify.
questions.a: No. -2, -4, -4 = -2 times (1, 2, 2), so the two sets are proportional and are direction ratios of the same line (or of parallel lines). Both give the direction cosines 1/3, 2/3, 2/3 up to sign.
s: Shows the two sets are proportional (factor -2)
Concludes they describe the same or parallel lines, e.g. both give direction cosines 1/3, 2/3, 2/3 up to sign

questions.q: Construct a set of three non-zero integer direction ratios for a line whose direction cosines are all rational numbers. Write both sets of direction cosines of the line and verify that l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1.
questions.a: For example 2, 3, 6: sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. The direction cosines are 2/7, 3/7, 6/7 or -2/7, -3/7, -6/7. Check: 4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 49/49 = 1. (1, 2, 2 with divisor 3 also works.)
s: Gives non-zero integer direction ratios whose sum of squares is a perfect square
Writes both sets of direction cosines (opposite signs)
Verifies the sum of squares is 1

concepts.name: Direction cosines of a line through two points and collinearity
concepts.description: Direction ratios and direction cosines of the line joining P(x1, y1, z1) and Q(x2, y2, z2), and the use of proportional direction ratios with a common point to show three points are collinear.
concepts.idea: Exactly one line passes through two points, and the differences of their coordinates give its direction ratios.
concepts.rule: Direction ratios of PQ: x2 - x1, y2 - y1, z2 - z1 (or the negatives). Direction cosines: these divided by PQ = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2). A, B, C are collinear if the direction ratios of AB and BC are proportional.
concepts.example: For P(-2, 4, -5) and Q(1, 2, 3): direction ratios 3, -2, 8, PQ = sqrt(77), direction cosines 3/sqrt(77), -2/sqrt(77), 8/sqrt(77).

wrong, because it gives a line perpendicular to PQ

questions.q: The points A(1, 2, 3), B(3, 5, 9) and C(5, p, q) are collinear. Find p and q.
questions.a: Direction ratios of AB are 2, 3, 6. Direction ratios of BC are 2, p - 5, q - 9. For collinearity these are proportional: 2/2 = (p - 5)/3 = (q - 9)/6, so p - 5 = 3 and q - 9 = 6. Hence p = 8 and q = 15.

Sets the two sets proportional

questions.q: For four points A, B, C, D a student finds that AB has direction ratios 1, 2, 3 and CD has direction ratios 2, 4, 6, and concludes that A, B, C, D all lie on one line. Evaluate this conclusion.
questions.a: The conclusion does not follow. Proportional direction ratios show only that AB is parallel to CD. Collinearity needs a common point as well (as B is common to AB and BC in the textbook method); AB and CD could be two distinct parallel lines.
s: States that proportional direction ratios prove only that AB is parallel to CD
Explains that a common point (e.g. checking BC as well) is needed, so the lines may be distinct parallel lines

questions.q: Construct three distinct points with integer coordinates, none of them the origin, that lie on one line with direction ratios 1, -2, 2. Verify the collinearity using direction ratios and write the direction cosines of the line.
questions.a: For example A(1, 1, 1), B(2, -1, 3), C(3, -3, 5). AB has direction ratios 1, -2, 2 and BC has direction ratios 1, -2, 2, which are proportional, and B is common, so the points are collinear. Since sqrt(1 + 4 + 4) = 3, the direction cosines are 1/3, -2/3, 2/3 (or all signs reversed).
s: Gives three valid distinct integer points, none the origin
Verifies direction ratios of AB and BC are proportional with B common
Writes the direction cosines 1/3, -2/3, 2/3 (or the opposite signs)

concepts.name: Equation of a line in space: vector and Cartesian forms
concepts.description: The vector equation r = a + lambda b of a line through a given point parallel to a given vector, its parametric and Cartesian forms, conversion between the forms, and the line through two points r = a + lambda (b - a).
concepts.idea: A line is fixed by one point on it and its direction. Every point of the line is reached from the given point by moving some multiple lambda of the direction vector.
concepts.rule: Vector form: r = a + lambda b. Cartesian form through (x1, y1, z1) with direction ratios a, b, c: (x - x1)/a = (y - y1)/b = (z - z1)/c, obtained by eliminating lambda from x = x1 + lambda a, y = y1 + lambda b, z = z1 + lambda c.
concepts.example: The line through (5, 2, -4) parallel to 3i + 2j - 8k is r = 5i + 2j - 4k + lambda (3i + 2j - 8k), i.e. (x - 5)/3 = (y - 2)/2 = (z + 4)/(-8).

questions.a: The required line is perpendicular to b1 = 3i - 16j + 7k and b2 = 3i + 8j - 5k, so it is parallel to b1 x b2 = (80 - 56)i - (-15 - 21)j + (24 + 48)k = 24i + 36j + 72k, i.e. to 2i + 3j + 6k. Hence r = i + 2j - 4k + lambda (2i + 3j + 6k).

questions.a: It is wrong: the student has interchanged the point and the direction. The point's coordinates are subtracted in the numerators and the direction ratios go in the denominators. The correct equation is (x - 4)/2 = (y + 3)/5 = (z - 1)/(-3).
s: Identifies that the point and the direction ratios have been interchanged

s: Writes a valid vector equation r = i + j + k + lambda b with three different positive integer components in b
Writes the matching Cartesian equation
Gives a correct second point for a stated value of lambda

concepts.name: Angle between two lines
concepts.description: The acute angle between two lines from their direction ratios, direction cosines or direction vectors, and the conditions for two lines to be perpendicular or parallel.
concepts.idea: The angle between two lines is the acute angle between their direction vectors; the points the lines pass through play no part. For skew lines, parallel lines through one point are used.
concepts.rule: cos theta = |a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2| / (sqrt(a1^2 + b1^2 + c1^2) sqrt(a2^2 + b2^2 + c2^2)) = |b1 . b2| / (|b1| |b2|); with direction cosines cos theta = |l1 l2 + m1 m2 + n1 n2|. Perpendicular: a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 = 0. Parallel: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2.
concepts.example: For direction vectors i + 2j + 2k and 3i + 2j + 6k: cos theta = (3 + 4 + 12)/(3 x 7) = 19/21.

concepts.name: Skew lines and the shortest distance between them
concepts.description: Skew lines as non-coplanar lines that are neither parallel nor intersecting, the line of shortest distance perpendicular to both, and the shortest distance in vector and Cartesian form.
concepts.idea: Skew lines never meet and are not parallel. The shortest segment joining them is perpendicular to both, so it lies along b1 x b2, and its length is the projection of any joining vector a2 - a1 on that direction.
concepts.rule: d = |(b1 x b2) . (a2 - a1)| / |b1 x b2| for the lines r = a1 + lambda b1 and r = a2 + mu b2. Intersecting lines have d = 0.
